2.4.title: Proposal Summary
lines: This project aims to give visitors to Warokutal (Safari Camp) access to water, supplies and vehicle recovery equipment when floods damage the roads. It proposes an elevated, low maintenance shelter that stocks essentials and hires out recovery kits, personal locator beacons and ultra high frequency radios.

2.5.title: Overview of design: summary
lines: The design achieves emergency flood resilience and supply security through an elevated, low maintenance shelter design equipped with lockable storage vaults, and self-service recovery gear distribution racks.

The implementation of this design is supported through prefabricated durable building components, local community partnerships to aid with stocking and maintenance, and clear signage guiding users when flooding occurs.

The physical components of the design include an elevated stilt mounted platform designed to remain above peak flood levels, a weatherproof secure storage shed that contains non-perishable food and drink, equipment lockers for PLB’s, UHF radios and vehicle recovery kits, and most importantly, solar powered lighting and battery-charging stations to ensure visibility and access during day or night.

Visitors, traditional owners and rangers traveling through Warokutal will use this facility, either during or immediately after severe floods when unsealed roads become unusable, stranding travellers without immediate access to rescue services.

2.8.title: Key Considerations
lines: Where the recommended materials are sourced from? (i.e. externally or locally available)

Heavy duty galvanised steel posts and fiber-cement or marine-grade aluminium cladding sourced from regional industrial hubs to be able to resist corrosion and termite damage. They will be sourced in bulk from trusted regional suppliers, with stock that will be rotated on a seasonal wet-season schedule.
What are the key maintenance requirements?

Annual structural inspections before wet seasons to make sure all is good, inventory audis every 6 months, water flitration units, and communication equipment batteries, and clear operational guidelines and user accountability protocols for borrowed vehicle recovery gear and PLB’s.
How do you propose the design might be implemented?
Community consultation with Lama Lama Traditional Owners and local land councils to finalise placement and cultural protocols.
Prefabrication of structural parts off-site to minimise environmental disturbance on Lama Lama country.
Assembly on-site by local work crews supported by specialised contractors, utilising light machinery.
What additional consultation/feedback/research might be required to validate your design proposal? What might the next steps be to make this idea happen?
Conduction water assessments with Traditional Owners to determine precise historical flood heights for best and optimal elevation.

5.1.title: Why this project matters
lines: Visitors to Warokutal need dependable access to water, supplies, recovery equipment and safety information when roads are damaged and help is far away.

5.2.title: Context
lines: Warokutal is a campground at Port Stewart in Lama Lama Country. Wet-season floods can damage the roads and other infrastructure (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2024). Visitors are far from services, so a stuck vehicle can become an emergency. The Lama Lama Rangers manage tourism and carry out repairs (Reardon-Smith, 2023). Their time is limited.

5.3.title: The design opportunity
lines: The EWB Challenge brief asks teams to design resilient infrastructure for a specific visitor destination in Lama Lama Country, such as a campground, creek crossing, boat ramp or visitor information point. The design must respond to wet-season flooding, visitor access, safety or maintenance needs, suit the expected visitor numbers, improve the visitor experience, and not harm cultural or environmental values (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2024).

5.4.title: How might we statement
lines: How might we make a Lama Lama Country campground safer for visitors, more resilient to floods and unreliable roads, with low capital investment and without adding more maintenance duties to Rangers, while protecting the region's cultural and ecological values?

6.1.title: Climate and flooding
lines: Heavy rain can flood roads and low ground across northern Cape York (Testa, 2026). The Lama Lama Rangers carry out infrastructure repairs (Reardon-Smith, 2023). Flood damage can therefore last after the water has gone.

6.2.title: Existing infrastructure and safety
lines: There are two campgrounds, Warokutal at Port Stewart and Maramba at Silver Plains, three boat ramps and one staffed information point, the Lama Lama Ranger Base. A single road joins Port Stewart to Coen (Cook Shire Council, 2026; Engineers Without Borders Australia, n.d.).

6.3.title: Visitors and experience
lines: Visitors come for bird watching, boating, fishing, camping and guided tours. The dry season brings most of them. The park is closed from 1 December to 30 June. The open season runs from July to November (Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation [DETSI], 2024b). TEAM TO ADD: confirm the park closure dates apply to Warokutal.

6.4.title: Tourism economy and maintenance
lines: Rangers manage tourism and carry out infrastructure repairs (Reardon-Smith, 2023). YAC earns income from tourism and from the YM2 cattle enterprise (YAC, n.d.). Ranger time is limited, so new infrastructure must not add much work.

6.5.title: Cultural values and protocols
lines: The Lama Lama people are the Traditional Owners. The Alingina Wungku Living Area is closed to visitors to protect cultural resources (YAC, n.d.). Entry to areas of high cultural or environmental value is limited to Traditional Owners or permit holders (Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [QPWS], 2013).

6.6.title: Ecological and environmental values
lines: Infrastructure is banned outright in the Alingina Wungku Living Area, the Goose Swamp and the Bull Swamp Area (QPWS, 2013). No camping development is permitted inside the national park.

6.7.title: Current practices
lines: Roads and other infrastructure are repaired when something breaks, not on a set schedule (Reardon-Smith, 2023). It is up to visitors to check road conditions on the Cook Shire Council website before they travel (Cook Shire Council, 2026). Entry to areas of high environmental or cultural value is limited to Traditional Owners or permit holders (QPWS, 2013).

6.8.title: Existing solutions
lines: Camping is kept outside the national park boundary, at the campgrounds of Warokutal and Maramba (DETSI, 2024a). Visitors currently need to bring their own recovery equipment. The Lama Lama Ranger Base at Port Stewart is the only staffed information point.

6.9.title: Why this is not enough
lines: These measures leave a gap. A visitor who is stuck at Warokutal must wait for help from the Ranger Base, which is far away and has limited staff. The team wants visitors to be able to recover their own vehicles, get water and supplies close by, and call for help, without adding to Ranger workload.

7.1.title: User needs statement
lines: User needs statement: Visitors to Lama Lama Country need consistent access to essential supplies, water and safety information so they can manage the risks of remote travel, unpredictable weather and extended stays.

7.2.title: The problem and the ideal situation
lines: Wet-season floods can damage the roads to Warokutal, and flood damage can last into the dry season. Visitors are far from services, so a stuck vehicle can become an emergency. The only staffed information point is the Lama Lama Ranger Base, and Ranger time is limited. The ideal situation is that visitors can recover their own vehicles, call for help and get water close by, while the design stays low cost, adds little work for Rangers and protects cultural and ecological values.

8.1.title: Criterion 1: Safety and access
lines: Criterion 1: Safety and access
The design must lower the risk of vehicles becoming stranded and help visitors recover or call for help. It must reduce reliance on Rangers.
Reason: visitors rely on one road, and Rangers run the one staffed safety point.

8.2.title: Criterion 2: Flood resilience
lines: Criterion 2: Flood resilience
The building and its stock must survive wet-season flooding with little repair.
Reason: floods can damage roads and infrastructure, and Rangers carry out the repairs.

8.3.title: Criterion 3: Visitor support and comfort
lines: Criterion 3: Visitor support and comfort
Visitors can get water, food, firewood and safety information near the campground.
Reason: stays are remote and long, so basic supplies cut risk and improve the visit.

8.4.title: Criterion 4: Feasibility and maintenance
lines: Criterion 4: Feasibility and maintenance
The design uses tough, durable materials and needs close to zero wet-season maintenance.
Reason: Ranger time is limited.

8.5.title: Criterion 5: Culture and Country
lines: Criterion 5: Culture and Country
The design respects heritage and fits the land management goals of the Traditional Owners.
Reason: no option would go ahead without Traditional Owner agreement.

8.6.title: Criterion 6: Low cost
lines: Criterion 6: Low cost
The design must be affordable to set up and run.
Reason: a grant would pay for the build, and sales and hire fees would pay for running costs.

8.7.title: Criterion 7: Community fit
lines: Criterion 7: Community fit
The design must suit the small, self-sufficient visitors to Port Stewart, such as campers and fishers, and not mass tourism.
Reason: the stock and kits suit small groups.

8.8.title: Criterion 8: Revenue
lines: Criterion 8: Revenue
The design should earn income of its own.
Reason: income would help fund the Lama Lama Rangers.

9.1.title: Introduction to the options
lines: The team developed four ideas and scored them against the eight criteria. The three highest scoring ideas are the design options below. Screened out: a solar-powered river crossing status beacon scored lowest (91 out of 165). It would warn drivers. TEAM TO ADD: confirm this description.

9.2.title: 3.1. Design option 1: Provisions Point
lines: The Provisions Point is a flood-resilient facility designed to provide visitors with essential supplies and emergency equipment during wet-season flooding. The proposed structure features an elevated platform, weather-resistant storage facilities, and secure compartments containing drinking water, non-perishable food, first-aid supplies, and vehicle recovery equipment. Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios would also be available to support emergency communication. This solution aims to improve visitor safety and access to essential resources while creating potential revenue opportunities through equipment rental.

9.3.title: 3.2. Design option 2: Elevated tent-site platform
lines: The Elevated Tent-site Platform proposes raised camping platforms designed to reduce visitors' exposure to ground-level flooding and wet conditions. The platforms would provide stable areas for setting up tents, potentially reducing damage to camping equipment and improving camping conditions during periods of heavy rainfall.

This solution focuses primarily on providing a safer camping environment rather than supplying emergency resources. Its relatively simple design could reduce initial construction costs, while its elevated structure offers improved flood resilience compared with ground-level campsites. However, the platforms would provide limited access to emergency supplies, communication equipment, and vehicle recovery services.

9.4.title: 3.3. Design option 3: Distributed emergency checkpoint
lines: The Distributed Emergency Checkpoint proposes a network of small emergency support stations positioned at selected locations around Warokutal. Each checkpoint could contain basic emergency supplies, safety information, and communication equipment, allowing visitors to access assistance without relying on a single central facility.

By distributing emergency resources across multiple locations, this solution aims to improve accessibility and provide support to visitors who may become stranded during flooding. The stations could also be adapted to local environmental and community requirements.

10.1.title: How the team chose
lines: Each idea was rated from 1 (poor) to 5 (best) against the eight criteria. Each criterion has a weight from 3 to 5, where 5 matters most. Weighted score is rating times weight. The maximum score is 165. Why the weights differ: Visitor support, feasibility and flood resilience carry weight 5, because a shelter that is unusable, impossible to build or flooded fails the brief. Culture and Country has weight 3 in the matrix, but it is also a condition for every option. No option would go ahead without Traditional Owner agreement.

11.1.title: Why it should work
lines: Safety and access: visitors could recover their own vehicles, call for help and get water close by. The Ranger Base is not the only point of help. Flood resilience: the building is raised and made of concrete and steel, so it should need little upkeep after the wet season. An engineer must confirm this. Culture and Country: one hub on cleared ground keeps foot traffic away from restricted sites, and the team proposes that YAC co-designs how it runs.

11.2.title: Note on the 2 m height
lines: Note on the 2 m height: this is a planning figure. An engineer must confirm it against local flood levels and wind loads.

11.3.title: How Provisions Point would work: What it is
lines: A 24 square metre shelter at Warokutal, planned for ground that is already cleared and above flood level. A site survey must confirm this. It would stand on reinforced concrete piles (Menard Asia, 2025), with the floor planned 2 m above the ground. Walls would be watertight concrete (Leading Architecture, 2024) and the roof corrugated sheeting (material to be confirmed). Inside would be shelves, a counter, a solar panel and a battery. The shelter is unstaffed. Visitors serve themselves and pay by the method YAC sets.

11.4.title: How Provisions Point would work: Entry, stock and hire items
lines: Entry: TEAM TO ADD: confirm the entry type (stairs or ramp) so it matches the prototype.
Stock: drinking water, non-perishable food, firewood and safety information.

Hire items: traction boards for soft ground, a tyre deflation kit (Supercheap Auto, 2017), a 12 V compressor, and shackles with a recovery strap (Bober, 2025). Each kit also holds a personal locator beacon (PLB) and an ultra high frequency (UHF) radio. YAC sets the check-out and payment method. One option is a lockable kit cage with a code given at booking.

11.5.title: How Provisions Point would work: How a visitor would use it
lines: 1. Check road conditions on the Cook Shire Council website before travel (Cook Shire Council, 2026).
2. Arrive at Warokutal and read the safety information at the shelter.
3. Buy water, food or firewood, or hire a recovery kit if the vehicle is stuck.
4. In a life-threatening emergency, use the PLB. If radio coverage is confirmed, the UHF radio can reach the Rangers. Then return the kit.

11.6.title: How Provisions Point would work: Community concerns
lines: Ground disturbance. The design uses a small number of drilled piles on cleared ground, not trench footings. No piles are drilled until Traditional Owners and heritage checks agree.
Ranger workload. The routine would be one weekly restock in the open season and two inspections a year.
Visitor numbers. The stock and kits suit small groups. The design is not for mass tourism.
Theft or damage. The team proposes a lockable, raised building for the stock and kits.
Fire and waste. Bagged firewood would be sold, and the team will check park rules with YAC and QPWS. A waste plan would be agreed with YAC.
Cost. A grant would pay for the build. Sales and hire fees would pay for running costs.

13.1.title: Implementation plan
lines: 1. Preparation. YAC approval would take about 6 months. The site, design and running plan are agreed with YAC and Traditional Owners. Cultural heritage checks come before any ground work.

2. Implementation. Four workers would build the shelter in the dry season in about 8 weeks, using a drill rig, steel and roof sheets. Each Ranger who will look after the site completes 4 hours of training.
3. Operation. The shelter would run during the open season, July to November (DETSI, 2024b). Rangers restock it weekly.
4. Maintenance. Two Rangers carry out two checks a year, one before and one after the wet season.
5. End of life. Four workers remove the building in 1 to 2 weeks. Shelves and kits are reused. Steel and roof sheets are recycled.

13.2.title: Community, ownership and evaluation
lines: Community role: the team proposes that YAC co-designs the site and the rules, and decides which of these steps go ahead. The team encourages YAC to consider local people for the build and training.
Ownership: the team proposes that YAC owns the shelter, sets prices and decides stock. Income would help fund the Lama Lama Rangers.
Evaluation: after each open season YAC and Rangers would review kit hires, visitor numbers, empty shelves, uses of the beacons and radios, and Ranger time. They would adjust stock and prices.
Repairs: Rangers fix small faults at the weekly and twice-yearly visits. Larger repairs use local trades. YAC and Rangers should agree a repair budget.
Future: if it works, the same model could be tried at Maramba.

13.3.title: Project stages
lines: Next steps: co-design with YAC, a site survey, engineering design, and checks on beacon hire rules and radio coverage.
The design is a student proposal. It is for YAC to review, change or reject.
Stage 1: Consultation with YAC and Traditional Owners. Duration: part of about 6 months of approval.
Stage 2: Cultural heritage and site checks. Duration: part of about 6 months of approval.
Stage 3: Engineering design. Flood and wind loads confirmed.
Stage 4: Grant application. About $86,650 for the build and equipment.
Stage 5: Dry-season build. Four workers, about 8 weeks.
Stage 6: Ranger training. 4 hours per Ranger.
Stage 7: Open season. July to November, weekly restock.
Stage 8: Review. Annual check by YAC and Rangers.

15.1.title: Stakeholders and what is not yet checked
lines: Stakeholders: YAC (owner and decision maker), Traditional Owners, the Lama Lama Rangers, visitors, Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service and Cook Shire Council.
Not yet checked: land tenure and building approval, park rules for selling goods, personal locator beacon (PLB) hire rules, and insurance and liability for hired equipment. YAC should advise on each.

15.2.title: Visitor journey
lines: Visitor journey, with the main worry at each step:
1. Plan: check road conditions and park rules. Worry: will the road be open?
2. Arrive: read the safety information, buy supplies. Worry: are there enough supplies?
3. Stuck: hire a kit and recover the vehicle. Worry: cost and time.
4. Emergency: use the PLB, or the radio if coverage is confirmed. Worry: will help come?
5. Leave: return the kit and give feedback.

15.3.title: Ranger journey
lines: Ranger journey:
1. Before the season: train and stock the shelter.
2. Each week: restock and check kits.
3. Twice a year: inspect before and after the wet season.

15.4.title: Community reaction
lines: Community reaction: The team has not yet asked YAC or Traditional Owners for their views. TEAM TO ADD: confirm this sentence is true, or add feedback received. Likely concerns are ground disturbance, extra Ranger work, visitor behaviour, theft and fire. This proposal is based on public sources and the EWB Challenge brief. It still needs to be checked with YAC and Traditional Owners.

15.5.title: Wider issues
lines: Wider issues: waste from packaging, weeds and pests carried in firewood (use commercial bagged wood and check park rules), fire risk, theft, and wildlife safety. Safety flyers should warn visitors about estuarine crocodiles and say that swimming is unsafe. TEAM TO ADD: citation for the official crocodile warning.

3. Get flood level data and an engineer's design for flood and wind loads. Confirm the roof material.

4. Confirm the rules for hiring out beacons with the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, and test UHF radio coverage between Warokutal and the Ranger Base. TEAM TO ADD: citation for the beacon rules.
